quote: I’ve spent some time online trying to track down the exact moment when someone noticed the vastly tangled internal structure of the brain’s neurons, and said, “Hey, I bet all this giant tangle is doing complex information-processing!” I haven’t had much luck.
content: The candidate is Alexander Bain, whose Mind and Body (1873) proposed that memories are stored in the pattern of connection strengths among nerve cells, that the same cells participate in many memories, and that learning consists of the growth of new junctions, a connectionist account complete enough that it has been described as anticipating Hebb (Wilkes & Wade (1997)). William James’s Principles of Psychology (1890, ch. XVI) has a wiring diagram of associative connections among “brain-processes.” Earlier still, Hartley’s Observations on Man (1749) explained association by vibrations propagating in the nerves, and Cabanis (1802) said the brain secretes thought as the liver secretes bile, which is a crude reduction but a reduction. None of these is hard to find, and the essay’s use of its own failed search as evidence that “maybe there was never a watershed moment” is an argument from the limits of a Google session, in a book that elsewhere insists absence of evidence be weighed by how hard one looked.

quote: It’s the point where you can look at a puppy, and say: “The puppy’s parents may push it to the ground when it does something wrong, but that doesn’t mean the puppy is doing moral reasoning. Our current theories of evolutionary psychology holds that moral reasoning arose as a response to more complex social challenges than that—in their full-fledged human form, our moral adaptations are the result of selection pressures over linguistic arguments about tribal politics.”
content: Two things are wrong. “Our current theories” is one theory, the argumentative or coalitional account, and it competes with accounts on which the building blocks of morality (empathy, reciprocity, consolation, inequity aversion) are shared with other mammals and predate language: de Waal’s program (de Waal (2008)) and the primate and canine experiments that followed it. On the puppy specifically, dogs show inequity aversion in a controlled task, refusing to continue working when a partner is rewarded and they are not (Range et al. (2009)), and the developmental literature finds precursors of moral evaluation in human infants before language (Hamlin, Wynn & Bloom (2007)). The puppy is not doing moral reasoning in the sense of arguing about tribal politics; nobody said it was. The essay uses it as the example of a case where anthropomorphism is “obviously stupid,” and the field’s finding is that the specific attribution at issue, that the puppy is tracking fairness and responding to correction as such, is roughly right.

quote: It’s the point where you can look at a tree, and say: “I don’t see anything in the tree’s biology that’s doing complex information-processing. Nor do I see it in the behavior, and if it’s hidden in a way that doesn’t affect the tree’s behavior, how would a selection pressure for such complex information-processing arise?”
content: One does see it, if one looks. Plants integrate light quality, gravity, touch, water status, herbivore damage and airborne volatiles from neighbours into growth and defence decisions; they propagate electrical signals, including action potentials, over long distances; they allocate resources between competing sinks in ways that respond to expected return; and there is a substantial literature on what should be called plant intelligence in the information-processing sense (Trewavas (2003)), with a live and hostile debate over whether any of it warrants the vocabulary of cognition or consciousness (Taiz et al. (2019), against). The essay’s own criterion, that selection would favour information-processing only where it affects behaviour, is met: plants behave, slowly, and the processing affects the behaviour. The right conclusion is the one the sceptics of plant cognition reach, that trees do not think because they have no nervous system and no central integration of the kind that supports thought; the essay reaches it by denying that the tree is processing anything, which is the animist’s error in reverse, dismissing what one has not examined.

We do not. Whether fish have affective states, including enjoyment, is an open scientific question with a literature on both sides. The case for fish pain and pleasure rests on nociceptors, behavioural changes reversed by analgesics, and learning (Sneddon, Braithwaite & Gentle (2003); Braithwaite, Do Fish Feel Pain?, 2010); the case against rests on the absence of a neocortex and arguments that the behavioural evidence shows nociception without experience (Key (2016), with several dozen published commentaries disagreeing). The dispute is not resolved by knowing that brains process information, which is all the essay has offered; it turns on what kind of processing supports what, and that is the hard question the rest of this sequence is about. Zhuangzi’s point was that Huizi’s demand for certainty about other minds could not be met from the outside; the essay answers him with a claim of knowledge that the relevant science does not make.
